questions.text: In the command ls -lr /labs, match each piece to what it is.
allChoices: The command — the base program you are executing
The options/flags — they tweak the command's behavior
The argument — the specific file or directory the command acts upon

pairs.match: The command — the base program you are executing
The options/flags — they tweak the command's behavior
The argument — the specific file or directory the command acts upon

questions.explanation: Slide “The Anatomy of a Command”: the action, the modifier and the target.

questions.text: How do you read the full manual for a command, and how do you leave it again?
options: man [command], then press q to quit
info [command], then press Ctrl+C to quit
help [command], then press Esc to quit
doc [command], then press x to quit
questions.explanation: The tip on the “Anatomy of a Command” slide: most commands support --help for a quick summary, or man [command] for the full manual — press q to quit.

questions.text: What does pwd do?
options: Prints the contents of the working directory
Prints the directory you are currently in, like a “You Are Here” pin
Returns you to your home directory
Changes your password
questions.explanation: Slide “Level 1: The Explorer”: pwd acts as a “You Are Here” pin on the map, e.g. /home/devasc/Documents. (It stands for print working directory — not password.)

questions.text: Fill in the command that teleports you straight back to the root of the file system.
questions.explanation: cd / jumps to the root node at the very top of the tree, from wherever you are.

questions.text: What does cd .. do?
options: Moves exactly one level up the tree, e.g. from Documents back to devasc
Moves to your home directory
Moves to the root of the file system
Moves to the previous directory you visited
questions.explanation: Slide “Level 1: The Explorer”: cd .. “moves the dot exactly one node up the tree”. Jumping all the way to the root is cd /.

questions.text: cd Documents works no matter how you capitalize the folder name.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The slide notes that cd into a specific folder “requires exact case sensitivity” — Linux treats Documents and documents as different names.

questions.text: Which key auto-completes a path after you type the first few letters of a directory?
options: Enter
Tab
Esc
Ctrl
questions.explanation: The pro-tip on the “Level 1: The Explorer” slide.

questions.text: Match each ls variation to what it shows.
allChoices: The default view — just the basic names
Peeks inside one specific folder
The long display — permissions, owner, size and date
The same names in reverse alphabetical order
The long display, in reverse alphabetical order

pairs.match: The default view — just the basic names
Peeks inside one specific folder
The long display — permissions, owner, size and date
The same names in reverse alphabetical order
The long display, in reverse alphabetical order

questions.explanation: Slide “Illuminating the Environment”. Verified by running each one: ls listed a.f b.f c.f, ls -r listed c.f b.f a.f.

questions.text: Fill in the flags that give a long listing in reverse alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: Stacking power: -l (long format) plus -r (reverse alphabetical) is written -lr.

questions.text: In this listing, what does the very first character of -rwxr-xr-x tell you?
options: It is a directory — a d there would mean a device
The file is empty
The owner has no read permission
It is a file — a d there would mean a directory
questions.explanation: Slide “The Permission String Decoder”: character 1 is the file type — a dash means it's a file, a d means it's a directory.

questions.text: Match each part of the permission string -rwxr-xr-x to what it controls.
allChoices: The file type
The owner's permissions
The group's permissions
Public/other permissions

pairs.match: The file type
The owner's permissions
The group's permissions
Public/other permissions

questions.explanation: Slide “The Permission String Decoder”.

questions.text: Match each permission letter to what it grants.
allChoices: Read
Write
Execute

pairs.match: Read
Write
Execute

questions.explanation: The owner block rwx on the “Permission String Decoder” slide.

questions.text: In -rwxr-xr-x 1 devasc devasc, what is the second devasc?
options: The user who last modified the file
The group that owns the file
The user who owns the file
The directory the file lives in
questions.explanation: Slide “The Permission String Decoder”: “First instance is the User (Owner). Second instance is the Group.”

questions.text: What does chmod +x myfile.sh do?
options: Makes the file readable by everyone
Removes write permission from the group
Grants execution rights, which is what fixes a “Permission denied” error
Marks the file as executable only for the root user
questions.explanation: Slide “Manipulating the Environment” — “The Key Maker”.

questions.text: What does sudo chown root myfile.sh do?
options: Gives root permission to read the file, leaving the owner unchanged
Moves the file into root's home directory
Transfers ownership of the file from the current user to root
Runs the file as root
questions.explanation: Slide “Manipulating the Environment” — “The Title Deed”. It needs sudo because changing an owner is a privileged operation.

questions.text: Match each file-manipulation command to what it does.
allChoices: Duplicates the file to a new name
Moves the file elsewhere (or renames it)
Permanently removes the file from the system
Grants execution rights on the file
Transfers ownership of the file to another user

pairs.match: Duplicates the file to a new name
Moves the file elsewhere (or renames it)
Permanently removes the file from the system
Grants execution rights on the file
Transfers ownership of the file to another user

questions.explanation: The five boxes on the “Manipulating the Environment” slide.

questions.text: mv is also how you rename a file, if the destination stays in the same folder.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — “The Transporter” box: mv moves a file across the map, and is “also used to rename files if kept in the same folder”.

questions.text: What is the difference between > and >>?
options: > adds to the end of the file; >> overwrites it
> writes to a file; >> writes to another command
> overwrites the file's contents; >> adds to the end of it
They are identical — >> is just the older spelling
questions.explanation: Slide “Controlling the Flow of Output”. Verified by running both: echo 'Linux is AWESOME!' > linux.txt followed by echo 'Linux is POWERFUL!' > linux.txt leaves only the second line, while the same pair with >> leaves both.

questions.text: Fill in the operator that adds this line to linux2.txt without erasing what is already in it.
questions.explanation: >> appends. > would wipe out “Linux is AWESOME!” and leave only the new line.

questions.text: What does cat linux2.txt do?
options: Creates the file if it does not exist
Concatenates the file onto the end of another one
Counts the lines in the file
Displays the contents of the file
questions.explanation: Slide “Controlling the Flow of Output” — “The Inspector” uses cat to confirm what actually landed in the file.

questions.text: In vi, which key takes you back to Command mode?
options: a
i
Esc
questions.explanation: Slide “The Vi Editor Engine”: Command mode (the default) is triggered by Esc; Edit mode by i (insert) or a (append).

questions.text: Match each vi Command-mode key to what it does.
allChoices: Delete (cut) the current line
Yank (copy) the current line
Put (paste) the line
Write (save) the file
Quit the editor

pairs.match: Delete (cut) the current line
Yank (copy) the current line
Put (paste) the line
Write (save) the file
Quit the editor

questions.explanation: Slide “The Vi Editor Engine”. In practice the line-wise delete and yank are typed twice — dd and yy — which is what the deck's single letters are shorthand for.

questions.text: You can save and quit from vi's Edit mode without going back to Command mode.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False — the Edit mode box says plainly: “You cannot save or quit from this mode.” Press Esc first, then :w / :q.

questions.text: grep is case-sensitive by default.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — slide “Level 3: The Detective”: grep devasc /etc/passwd highlights devasc and explicitly skips DEVASC.

questions.text: Match each regular-expression symbol to what it matches.
allChoices: The beginning of a line
The end of a line
Any single character — a fixed-length wildcard
A range of numbers or characters
Zero or more of the preceding pattern

pairs.match: The beginning of a line
The end of a line
Any single character — a fixed-length wildcard
A range of numbers or characters
Zero or more of the preceding pattern

questions.explanation: The Regex Anchor Table. Verified by running each against a sample file.

questions.text: Fill in the anchor that returns only the lines of /etc/passwd that start with root.
questions.explanation: The caret anchors the match to the beginning of the line. Verified: against a sample file, grep '^root' returned the root:x:0 line and skipped notroot.

questions.text: Which lines does grep 'd..m' match?
options: Any line starting with d and ending with m
Only daemon
Only lines that contain a literal d..m
Both daemon and dnsm
questions.explanation: Each dot is exactly one character, so d..m is d + any two + m: daem(on) and dnsm both qualify. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Which lines does grep 'false$' return?
options: Only the lines where false is the last thing on the line
Lines containing false followed by a dollar sign
Only the lines that begin with false
Every line containing the word false
questions.explanation: $ anchors to the end of the line. Verified: it matched the line false but not false ending.

questions.text: What does grep '[8-9]' return?
options: Lines containing every digit from 8 to 9 in order
Lines containing an 8, a 9, or both
Lines containing exactly eight or nine characters
Lines containing the literal text [8-9]
questions.explanation: Brackets are a number/character range. Verified against a sample file: it returned line8 and line9 and skipped line7.

questions.text: The deck says grep 'new*' matches both new and ne. Why does ne match?
options: * makes the whole pattern case-insensitive
* means zero or more of the preceding character, so the w is optional
grep falls back to a partial match when nothing matches exactly
* is a wildcard for any single character
questions.explanation: * applies to the character right before it — here w — and zero copies is allowed. Worth knowing: this makes the pattern match any line containing ne, which is exactly what happened when I ran it.

questions.text: What does the ip address command show about dummy0 holding 192.0.2.1 through 192.0.2.5?
options: That a single interface can host multiple IP addresses
That five separate interfaces are configured
That the interface is cycling through addresses via DHCP
That the addresses are aliases of the loopback interface
questions.explanation: Slide “Level 4: The Root Operator” — “A single interface can host multiple IP addresses.”

questions.text: What does the -c 4 in ping -c 4 192.168.1.1 do?
options: Limits the ping to 4 packets
Sends packets 4 bytes in size
Waits 4 seconds between packets
Retries 4 times if the host does not answer
questions.explanation: Slide “Level 4: The Root Operator” — the “Connectivity Radar” box. Without a count, ping keeps going until you stop it.

questions.text: Pinging www.cisco.com instead of an IP address triggers a DNS resolution first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — the note on that slide: pinging a domain “triggers an invisible DNS resolution first”, turning the name into an address before any packet is sent.

questions.text: In the output of ps -ef, what is PID 1?
options: [kthreadd], the kernel thread daemon
The oldest process belonging to your user
The shell you are typing in
/sbin/init, with a PPID of 0 — the root of the process tree
questions.explanation: Slide “Process Anatomy (ps -ef)” — “The Family Tree”: PID 1 (/sbin/init) | PPID: 0, with PID 2 ([kthreadd]) also at PPID 0 and PIDs 3, 4 and 6 hanging off PID 2.

questions.text: In ps -e | more, what is the pipe doing?
options: Halting the flood of output and presenting it one screen at a time
Running the two commands one after the other
Filtering the output down to the processes you own
Sending the output to a file called more
questions.explanation: Slide “Process Anatomy” — “The Output Valve”.

questions.text: While paging through output with more, what do Enter and Space each do?
options: Enter advances one line; Space advances one full screen
Both advance one full screen
Enter advances one full screen; Space advances one line
Enter quits; Space advances one line
questions.explanation: Slide “Process Anatomy” — “The Output Valve”.

questions.text: Match each step of the apt-get lifecycle to what it does.
allChoices: Syncs with the remote repository to refresh the list of available packages
Queries the local cache to find the exact package name
Fetches the dependencies and installs that specific package
Completely removes the package and frees the disk space

pairs.match: Syncs with the remote repository to refresh the list of available packages
Queries the local cache to find the exact package name
Fetches the dependencies and installs that specific package
Completely removes the package and frees the disk space

questions.explanation: Slide “The apt-get Lifecycle (Requires sudo)”, in order: refresh → discover → build → destroy.

questions.text: apt-get upgrade updates every package on the system, not just one.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — the note in step 3: “upgrade updates ALL system packages”, whereas install targets the one package you name.

questions.text: Which of these operations does the deck show being run through sudo? (Select three answers)
options: Searching /etc/passwd with grep
Listing a directory with ls -l
Purging a package with apt-get
Installing a package with apt-get
Changing a file's owner with chown
Printing the working directory with pwd
questions.explanation: The apt-get lifecycle slide is titled “Requires sudo”, and “The Title Deed” box shows sudo chown root myfile.sh. Navigation and reading commands need no elevation. (Note apt-cache search is the one step on that slide shown without sudo, since it only reads the local cache.)

questions.text: What does passwd -S do?
options: Reports the status of the current user's password
Shows every user's password hash
Sets a new password for the current user
Suspends the account until the next login
questions.explanation: Slide “System Control & Security” — “The Keycard”: plain passwd updates the password, passwd -S checks its status.

questions.text: In this passwd -S output, what does the 99999 mean?
options: The number of days the account stays active after expiry
The number of failed logins allowed
The maximum number of days before the password expires
The minimum number of days before the password may be changed
questions.explanation: Slide “System Control & Security”: 0 is the minimum days before a change is allowed, 99999 the maximum days before expiration, and -1 means the account stays active indefinitely after expiration. (The 7 the deck skips over is the number of days you are warned before expiry.)

questions.text: Match each shutdown form to what it does.
allChoices: Halts the operating system immediately
Schedules the halt one minute out and broadcasts a message to all active users
Cancels a shutdown that is already pending

pairs.match: Halts the operating system immediately
Schedules the halt one minute out and broadcasts a message to all active users
Cancels a shutdown that is already pending

questions.explanation: Slide “System Control & Security” — “The Kill Switch”.

questions.text: From the Operator's Toolkit summary, which commands belong to the “Search (The Detective)” group? (Select two answers)
options: cp
grep
cd
ps -ef
cat
chmod
questions.explanation: The final “Operator's Toolkit” slide groups the commands four ways: Navigate (pwd, cd, ls), Manipulate (cp, mv, rm, chmod, chown, >, >>), Search (cat, grep and the regex symbols) and Administer (sudo, apt-get, ps -ef, ip address, ping -c, shutdown).
